name: Red light mask (Omnilux/CurrentBody)

lead: Red light masks are wearable LED devices that illuminate the face with red (and sometimes near-infrared or blue) light. Brands such as Omnilux and CurrentBody sell them for home use, marketed for skin quality.
The general approach, called LED light therapy or photobiomodulation, has been studied in dermatology with mixed and often preliminary results.

paras: Encyclopedic descriptions say red and near-infrared light penetrate skin and act mainly on mitochondria, particularly cytochrome c oxidase, which proponents link to collagen production and reduced inflammation [1].
LED therapy is described as having fewer side effects than lasers; reported effects for low-level light include itching, red spots and mild allergic reactions, usually temporary [1].

studies.title: Effects of red light on sleep inertia.

lead: A red light mask is a consumer LED device worn over the face that emits red light, sometimes combined with near-infrared or blue wavelengths, and is marketed for wrinkles, acne, puffiness and general skin appearance. Omnilux and CurrentBody are brand names associated with such masks.

The technique belongs to LED light therapy, in which low-level non-coherent light is intended to stimulate cellular repair through a process called photobiomodulation [1]. Wikipedia describes research results as mixed and often preliminary [1].
No clinical trial of a specific Omnilux or CurrentBody mask was located for this article.

paras: Proponents and encyclopedic summaries describe photobiomodulation as low-level light acting mainly on mitochondria, especially cytochrome c oxidase, to stimulate repair and reduce inflammation [1]. Longer red and near-infrared wavelengths penetrate more deeply than blue or green light, which hemoglobin absorbs [1].
Red light is linked in the literature to collagen production, circulation and reduced inflammation, while blue light at about 415 nm has been used for acne [1].

LED therapy is generally described as having fewer side effects than lasers because the light is non-coherent and lower in intensity [1]. Reported effects of photobiomodulation include itching, red spots and mild allergic reactions, usually temporary [1].

Red light was originally developed partly for plant growth in space and for astronaut wound healing, and Niels Finsen's lamp for skin tuberculosis is often cited as the start of modern light therapy; LED use in cosmetology grew in the 1980s, particularly for acne [1].
No studies found. A search surfaced only a 2019 study of a red-light sleep mask on sleep inertia, which concerns alertness after waking rather than skin and is not relevant to facial appearance.
